title: Teaching and Learning are Worlds Apart
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles argues that schools pour their improvement effort into teacher coaching and technique training when the larger lever is the curriculum. He builds an extended analogy with ESG investing: just as divesting from polluting companies can make them less green and worsen total emissions, focusing on incremental teacher improvement yields only slight gains in learning. Teaching technique is a long list (Lemov alone offers over sixty techniques), while learning needs only three ingredients: content, hard thinking tasks, and being made to remember. All three are curriculum matters, so a ten percent curriculum improvement moves student progress ten percent, whereas a ten percent gain in every teacher might move it about one percent. He closes by urging leaders to invest CPD time in curriculum design instead.
points: Instructional coaching and Teach Like a Champion-style training improve one teacher at a time and, in the author's estimate, move student learning only slightly.
Learning requires only three things: content to engage with, tasks that make students think hard, and retrieval, spacing and interleaving, all of which live in the curriculum.
A shared curriculum improvement scales to every student at once, while teacher-by-teacher improvement is uneven and some CPD is misapplied or rejected.
The ESG investing analogy is used to show that pouring resources into the visibly 'green' activity (teaching technique) can be less effective than working on the hard, high-impact area.
quotes: When we focus on teaching, we only have a slight impact on learning. This is like the expensive investment in Green.

Every teacher has to improve. They do so at different rates. Many of the teaching techniques they improve in have a minimal impact on progress. Learning gets better, but slowly, and only by a little bit. This is like Green investing.

But, if we simply focus on whether and how students are learning - in class, for homework, and during assessments (yes, assessments make students learn, even if they never get feedback!) - then they will make so much more progress. This is Brown investing, because curriculum devours our finite resource - time. A better curriculum means students learn much more in the same time.

Learning happens when students do stuff. When they think hard. When they are made to remember. Sure, we can train teachers in all sorts of ways - Lemov gives us over 60. But with learning, we have only 3. Students do stuff - that is the curriculum content. They think hard - those are the tasks we set them - in class, at home, in assessments. The curriculum. They are made to remember

If we improve every teacher by 10%, this might have only a 1% impact on what students learn - there’s no improvement in the curriculum. So, a 1% improvement in progress. In reality, we will improve only some teachers by 10%, others will misunderstand, misapply or simply reject our CPD. But if we improve the curriculum by 10%, progress improves by 10%.
We visit lessons, we give teachers our expert Green advice and, if we are good leaders, Brown teaching disappears.
